items.prompt: What is the core structural difference between a pitch and a discovery conversation?
choices: In a pitch the seller talks and the buyer listens; in discovery the seller asks and the buyer talks
A pitch is shorter than a discovery conversation
Discovery only happens after a deal is already signed
A pitch uses a phone call while discovery only happens by email
items.reference:
🎤 Pitch — seller talks, buyer listens
👂 Discovery — seller asks, buyer talks

Why: Adri's fifteen-minute feature tour was a pitch from the first sentence; Bex's call stayed a question until Priya had described her own situation.
items.explanation: A pitch is built around the seller presenting information; discovery is built around the seller asking questions and the buyer describing their own situation. Who is talking, and who is being asked to talk, is the structural signal that separates the two.

items.prompt: Adri and Bex got the same lead, used the same product knowledge, and spoke for a similar amount of time. What actually explains why Bex closed a bigger deal?
choices: Bex structured the call around asking and listening before presenting anything
Bex offered a lower price
Bex had a more experienced engineering team backing the demo
Bex simply got lucky with an easier prospect
items.reference:
🎤 Pitch — seller talks, buyer listens
👂 Discovery — seller asks, buyer talks

Why: Adri's fifteen-minute feature tour was a pitch from the first sentence; Bex's call stayed a question until Priya had described her own situation.
items.explanation: Both reps had identical product knowledge and a similar-length call. The only real difference was the shape of the conversation: Bex asked before presenting, which is what let the real, bigger problem surface at all.

items.prompt: Why is pitching too early described as the most common way a deal ends up smaller than it could have been, or lost outright?
choices: It answers the prospect's stated ask before anyone finds out whether that's the real problem
It always uses the wrong pricing tier by default
It takes too much of the seller's time to prepare
It requires more slides than a discovery-first call
items.reference: The trap: a confident, accurate answer to the wrong problem still loses.
items.explanation: Pitching too early answers exactly what the prospect asked for in their own limited words, without checking whether that ask actually captures the real, often bigger, problem underneath it. A well-delivered pitch to the wrong problem still fails to land.

items.prompt: Priya originally asked for pricing on an 8-person tool. Why didn't pitching directly to that ask work well?
choices: Because it treated her first guess at the problem as the whole problem, instead of finding out what was underneath it
Because 8-person teams never buy project management tools
Because the price she was quoted was too high
Because Adri's screen share had a technical glitch
items.reference: The trap: a confident, accurate answer to the wrong problem still loses.
items.explanation: Priya's stated ask was a genuine first guess, not a lie — but it was shaped by what she'd experienced day to day, not by the full cross-team problem she hadn't been asked to describe yet. Pitching straight to the stated ask never gave that fuller picture a chance to surface.

items.prompt: Which of these is an open question, in the sense this unit uses the term?
choices: "Walk me through what happens today when a handoff between teams gets missed."
"Do you need better reporting?"
"Is 8 seats the right number for your team?"
"Would faster response times help you?"
items.reference:
✅ Open — no fixed answer shape, prospect supplies the content
⚠️ Closed — yes/no, assumption baked into the wording
items.explanation: An open question has no fixed answer shape and hands the floor to the prospect to describe something in their own words. The other three all presuppose an answer (reporting, seat count, response time) and only ask for a yes or no confirmation of it.

items.prompt: A rep asks: "So the main issue is speed, right?" What kind of question is this, despite sounding conversational?
choices: A closed question — it states an assumption and only asks for confirmation
An open question — it invites a detailed story
Neither — it's not a question at all
A need-payoff question
items.reference:
✅ Open — no fixed answer shape, prospect supplies the content
⚠️ Closed — yes/no, assumption baked into the wording
items.explanation: The assumption ("the main issue is speed") is already embedded in the question, so the prospect is only being asked to confirm or deny it — that's a closed question, regardless of its casual tone.

items.prompt: Why do open questions tend to surface a prospect's real, unstated problem better than closed ones?
choices: Because they let the prospect describe their situation in their own words, instead of confirming the seller's guess
Because they take less time to answer
Because prospects are legally required to answer them fully
Because they always mention pricing
items.reference:
✅ Open — no fixed answer shape, prospect supplies the content
⚠️ Closed — yes/no, assumption baked into the wording
items.explanation: An open question hands the floor to the prospect with no built-in assumption, so whatever comes back is genuinely theirs — often including details the seller had no way to guess in advance, which is exactly where an unstated problem tends to live.

items.prompt: What is the order of the four-step discovery flow this unit introduces?
choices: Situation, problem, implication, need-payoff
Problem, situation, need-payoff, implication
Pitch, price, close, follow-up
Implication, need-payoff, situation, problem
items.reference: Situation → Problem → Implication → Need-payoff — each step's questions build on the one before.
items.explanation: The flow moves from understanding the current setup (situation), to the specific friction in it (problem), to what that friction actually costs (implication), to the prospect stating in their own words what solving it would be worth (need-payoff).

items.prompt: Bex first asks Priya how work moves from her team through design and engineering. Which step of the four-step flow is this?
choices: Situation
Problem
Implication
Need-payoff
items.reference: Situation → Problem → Implication → Need-payoff — each step's questions build on the one before.
items.explanation: Asking how the current setup works, before touching anything that sounds like a problem, is the situation step — it establishes context so the next step's problem question can be sharp instead of generic.

items.prompt: Why does this unit treat asking good questions as a distinct, learnable skill rather than just "being a good listener"?
choices: Because the specific kind of question asked, and its order, determines what actually gets surfaced
Because listening isn't actually necessary if the questions are good enough
Because it's mostly about talking faster than the prospect
Because good listeners never need to ask any questions
items.reference: The point isn't more questions for their own sake — it's the right handful, in the right order.
items.explanation: Listening matters, but it only works on what actually gets said — and what gets said depends heavily on what was asked and in what order. A closed question and an open question invite fundamentally different answers even from the most attentive listener.

items.prompt: This unit warns against turning discovery into "an interrogation." What does that warning actually caution against?
choices: Asking many questions for their own sake instead of a handful of genuinely open ones
Ever asking more than one question per call
Taking notes during the conversation
Letting the prospect speak for more than a minute at a time
items.reference: The point isn't more questions for their own sake — it's the right handful, in the right order.
items.explanation: The goal is a handful of genuinely open questions that build understanding, not a long checklist of questions asked for volume's sake — an interrogation-style call is its own failure mode, separate from pitching too early.

items.prompt: How does this unit's discovery differ from `product-domain/requirements-gathering`?
choices: Discovery is the live conversation that surfaces what the ask even should be, often before it's stated; requirements-gathering starts from an ask that's already stated
They are two names for exactly the same process
Discovery only applies to existing customers, not prospects
Requirements-gathering happens earlier in the sales process than discovery
items.reference: Discovery is upstream: it surfaces the ask itself, often before the prospect has articulated it.
items.explanation: Requirements-gathering presupposes the ask already exists and turns it into something buildable. Discovery is a step upstream of that — it's the live conversation, often a first sales call, that surfaces what the real ask should be in the first place, sometimes before the prospect has put it into words themselves.

items.prompt: How does discovery relate to `product-domain/value-framing-over-feature-framing`?
choices: Discovery happens before the pitch and determines what to say; value-framing is about how to present once you already know what matters
They're the same skill applied at different price points
Value-framing replaces the need for discovery entirely
Discovery is only used after a deal has already been signed
items.reference: Discovery happens first and finds the real problem; framing happens after and presents the solution to it well.
items.explanation: Value-framing over feature-framing is about presenting a known value clearly once it's understood. Discovery is what determines, in the first place, what that value actually is for this specific prospect — it comes before framing can even start.

items.prompt: According to this unit, are closed questions always the wrong tool to use in a sales conversation?
choices: No — they're the right tool for confirming a detail once the real problem is already understood
Yes — closed questions should never be used at any point in a call
Yes, but only because they take longer to answer than open questions
No — closed questions should always come before open questions
items.reference: Closed questions confirm; open questions reveal. Each has a right moment — closed questions used too early just get the prospect nodding along to a guess.
items.explanation: Closed questions aren't inherently bad — they're well suited to confirming a specific detail late in a call, after the real problem is already understood. The failure mode is using them too early, before that understanding exists, where they just produce agreement with the seller's first guess.

items.prompt: A rep, late in a call, after Priya has already described the handoff problem in detail, asks "So a multi-team plan makes sense here?" Is this use of a closed question a mistake?
choices: No — it's confirming a detail after the real problem is already understood, which is exactly what closed questions are good for
Yes — closed questions are never appropriate anywhere in a discovery call
Yes — the rep should have asked an open question instead at this exact point
No, but only because the plan being confirmed is the cheaper one
items.reference: Closed questions confirm; open questions reveal. Each has a right moment — closed questions used too early just get the prospect nodding along to a guess.
items.explanation: This closed question comes after the open questions have already done the work of surfacing the real problem — at that point, a closed question is an efficient way to confirm a specific detail, not a shortcut around understanding.

items.prompt: A rep asks: "The main pain point is response time, right?" and the prospect says "yeah, I guess." What does this exchange actually demonstrate?
choices: A closed question wearing an open question's clothing, producing soft agreement rather than the prospect's own answer
A textbook open question that successfully surfaced the real problem
Proof that response time genuinely is the prospect's main concern
An implication question that quantified the cost of the problem
items.reference: "Yeah, I guess" is soft, uncommitted agreement to a framing the prospect didn't generate themselves — not a discovered answer.
items.explanation: The question states the seller's assumption and only asks for confirmation, so it's structurally closed even though it's phrased conversationally. "Yeah, I guess" is the telltale sign of someone accepting a handed-to-them framing rather than describing their own situation.

items.prompt: What would a genuinely open version of "The main pain point is response time, right?" look like?
choices: "What's been the most frustrating part of how this works today?"
"Is response time your main pain point, yes or no?"
"Would you agree response time matters to you?"
"Response time is the main pain point, correct?"
items.reference: "Yeah, I guess" is soft, uncommitted agreement to a framing the prospect didn't generate themselves — not a discovered answer.
items.explanation: An open version removes the seller's assumption entirely and asks the prospect to supply their own answer from their own situation, rather than confirming or denying a framing handed to them.

items.prompt: What is the actual purpose of the situation step, and what's the risk of overdoing it?
choices: It builds just enough context for a sharp problem question next; overdoing it risks it becoming unfocused small talk
It exists to make the prospect comfortable, and has no bearing on later questions
It's meant to fill time before the pitch begins
It should always take up more than half the call
items.reference: Flow: Situation → Problem → Implication → Need-payoff, each step earning the next.
items.explanation: The situation step exists to gather just enough context to ask a genuinely sharp problem question afterward — it's easy to over-invest in because it can feel like harmless small talk, but its value is entirely in what it sets up, not in itself.

items.prompt: Bex asks how many teams touch a piece of work before it's delivered, and learns the answer is three, not one. What does this situation-step answer change about the rest of the call?
choices: It reframes the scope of the problem from one team to three, which the original 8-person inquiry never revealed
Nothing — situation answers never affect later questions
It means the call should move straight to pricing
It proves the prospect doesn't actually need help
items.reference: Flow: Situation → Problem → Implication → Need-payoff, each step earning the next.
items.explanation: This single situation answer reframes everything that follows — a problem question aimed at "your 8-person team" would have missed the cross-team nature of the real friction entirely, which is exactly what the situation step exists to prevent.

items.prompt: What does the implication step add that the problem step alone doesn't?
choices: It surfaces what the friction actually costs, turning a stated problem into a felt, often urgent, cost
It restates the problem in different words for emphasis
It asks the prospect to name their budget directly
It is optional and can be skipped without losing anything
items.reference: A problem that sounds minor can have an implication that isn't minor at all — this is the step pitch-first conversations skip.
items.explanation: Naming a problem ("handoffs sometimes get missed") doesn't by itself convey how much it matters. The implication step asks what that problem actually costs — in Priya's case, $6,000 rush fees and a missed client launch — which is what turns a mild annoyance into a real, felt cost worth solving.

items.prompt: This unit calls the implication step "the step pitch-first conversations skip entirely." What's the practical consequence of skipping it?
choices: The pitch has to manufacture urgency on its own instead of relying on urgency the prospect already stated
The call simply runs shorter, with no other effect
The prospect is more likely to ask for a discount
The seller is legally required to lower the price
items.reference: A problem that sounds minor can have an implication that isn't minor at all — this is the step pitch-first conversations skip.
items.explanation: Without an implication answer on the table, urgency has to come entirely from the seller's side of the conversation — which is a much harder sell than urgency the prospect already put into their own words a moment earlier.

items.prompt: A rep asks the situation question, then the problem question, then jumps straight to the pitch. What did they skip, and what happens as a result?
choices: They skipped implication, leaving the prospect's urgency at whatever mild level it started, and the pitch has to manufacture urgency on its own
They skipped situation, which means the pitch will use the wrong product name
They skipped nothing — situation and problem are the only two steps that matter
They skipped need-payoff, which only affects the final invoice
items.reference: Skipping implication leaves urgency exactly where it started — mild — and removes the prospect's own anchor for judging the price that follows.
items.explanation: Naming a problem without also surfacing its cost leaves the prospect's sense of urgency unchanged. It also removes their anchor for judging whether the price that follows is reasonable, since there's no cost figure on the table to compare it against.

items.prompt: Why does skipping the implication step also make the price harder for the prospect to evaluate, not just the urgency?
choices: Without a cost figure on the table, the prospect has no anchor for judging whether the price that follows is reasonable
It doesn't affect price evaluation at all, only urgency
It means the price will automatically be quoted too high
It means the seller must offer a refund guarantee
items.reference: Skipping implication leaves urgency exactly where it started — mild — and removes the prospect's own anchor for judging the price that follows.
items.explanation: A stated implication cost (like $6,000 in rush fees) gives the prospect something concrete to weigh a price against. Without it, everything after that point in the call is guesswork on both sides, including whether the number quoted is reasonable.

items.prompt: In the need-payoff step, who is supposed to state why solving the problem matters?
choices: The prospect, in their own words, having just walked through the cost themselves
The seller, asserting it directly to the prospect
A third-party reference customer, quoted during the call
It's left unstated deliberately at this step
items.reference: A need-payoff answer spoken by the prospect is a stronger foundation for a pitch than anything the seller could assert unprompted.
items.explanation: The need-payoff question is designed so the prospect, not the seller, states the value out loud — because a value claim in the prospect's own words, arrived at through their own reasoning, is a far stronger foundation for the pitch that follows than an assertion from the seller's side.

items.prompt: Priya says a bigger, multi-team plan would be worth it to avoid another missed launch. Why does this answer, in her own words, matter more than if Bex had simply asserted the same thing?
choices: Because it's the prospect's own conclusion, reached by reasoning through her own situation and cost, not a claim she has to take on faith
Because it locks Priya into a legally binding commitment
It doesn't matter more — either version would work equally well
Because it means the price can now be raised without justification
items.reference: A need-payoff answer spoken by the prospect is a stronger foundation for a pitch than anything the seller could assert unprompted.
items.explanation: Priya reasoned her way to that conclusion through the previous three steps, which makes it something she believes rather than something she's being asked to accept. That's a meaningfully stronger foundation for the pitch that comes next.

items.prompt: According to the pitch-first vs. discovery-first comparison, what sets the ceiling on deal size in a pitch-first conversation?
choices: Whatever was originally asked for, since nothing in the call ever tests whether that ask was the real scope of the problem
The seller's personal sales quota for the month
The number of features shown in the demo
The length of the call in minutes
items.reference: Pitch-first caps the deal at the original ask; discovery-first lets the real problem's scope set the ceiling instead.
items.explanation: A pitch-first call answers the stated ask directly, so the deal it produces, if it closes at all, is capped at that original ask — there's no step in the conversation that tests whether the real problem is actually bigger.

items.prompt: Bex's eventual pitch to Priya is a single sentence before asking to demo. Why does such a short pitch work here?
choices: Because Priya already established the problem existed, mattered, and roughly what it was worth, so the pitch just needs to point at the matching capability
Because short pitches always outperform long ones regardless of context
Because Bex ran out of time on the call
Because Priya explicitly asked for a shorter pitch
items.reference: A short pitch here isn't a shortcut — the previous four questions already did the persuading.
items.explanation: By the time Bex pitches, Priya has already stated, in her own words, that the problem exists, that it's costly, and that a bigger solution would be worth it. The pitch doesn't need to establish any of that from scratch — it only needs to name the specific capability that matches what she just described.

items.prompt: Adri's pitch covered every feature of the product in case one of them mattered. What does the unit say a long, cover-everything pitch is often a symptom of?
choices: Not yet knowing what the prospect actually needs
A well-prepared, thorough sales process
A prospect who asked many detailed questions
A product with too few real capabilities
items.reference: A short pitch here isn't a shortcut — the previous four questions already did the persuading.
items.explanation: A pitch that tries to cover every feature, just in case one of them lands, is usually compensating for not yet knowing which capability actually matters to this specific prospect — the opposite of thoroughness, even though it can look like it.

items.prompt: A prospect responds to an implication question with "it's fine, we manage." What's the better next move, according to this unit?
choices: Make the question more concrete by referencing a specific memory or event, rather than dropping it or accepting the vague answer as final
Immediately move on to pricing since the prospect has no real problem
Repeat the exact same abstract question a second time
End the call, since a vague answer means the deal is dead
items.reference: A vague answer isn't a dead end — it's a sign to trade an abstract question for a specific, concrete one.
items.explanation: Trading an abstract cost question for a concrete, specific one ("you mentioned a missed launch date — what actually happened after that?") is usually easier for a prospect to answer honestly than a cold request to estimate a dollar figure, and it gives the vague answer a second, better chance to become real.

items.prompt: If a prospect still won't engage with cost even after a concrete, specific follow-up question, what does the unit say that might actually mean?
choices: The problem, real as it is, may not be painful enough yet to justify buying something to fix it
The rep is asking the questions in the wrong order
The prospect is lying about the problem existing at all
The product simply isn't a good fit for this industry
items.reference: A vague answer isn't a dead end — it's a sign to trade an abstract question for a specific, concrete one.
items.explanation: Continued non-engagement with cost, even after a concrete follow-up, is itself useful information — it can mean the problem, while real, isn't yet painful enough to justify action, and no amount of rephrasing will manufacture urgency that genuinely isn't there.

items.prompt: On a call with three stakeholders, an open question gets three different, even conflicting, answers. What does this unit say about that divergence?
choices: The divergence itself is useful information, often meaning the "real problem" is a cluster of related ones, not one single thing
It means the rep asked a badly worded question and should rephrase it
It should be ignored in favor of whichever answer came first
It means the deal is unlikely to close and should be deprioritized
items.reference: Divergent answers across stakeholders are a finding, not a problem to smooth over — they usually mean the real issue is a cluster, not one thing.
items.explanation: When different stakeholders answer the same open question differently, it's usually not a sign of a bad question — it's a sign that the real problem shows up differently for each of them, which is exactly the kind of finding discovery is meant to surface.

items.prompt: Why does this unit warn against only asking questions a multi-stakeholder group will comfortably agree on?
choices: Because it produces a shallower call, not a calmer one, by papering over real conflict instead of surfacing it
Because disagreement always means the deal is lost
Because agreement between stakeholders is illegal to record
Because it takes more time than asking divisive questions
items.reference: Divergent answers across stakeholders are a finding, not a problem to smooth over — they usually mean the real issue is a cluster, not one thing.
items.explanation: Sticking only to questions the group will agree on avoids visible friction in the moment, but it also means real, useful differences between stakeholders never surface — which produces a call that feels comfortable but leaves the actual picture incomplete.

items.prompt: The finance director gives a sharp, specific implication answer; the engineering lead gives a vague one to the same question. What's the honest move for the rep, in the moment?
choices: Notice the gap and ask about it directly, rather than building the pitch around only the sharper answer
Ignore the engineering lead's answer since it added no new information
Ask the finance director to repeat their answer more slowly
End the call and follow up with the engineering lead separately later, without mentioning it in the room
items.reference: A vague answer next to a sharp one is a real finding, not noise — worth naming in the room, not smoothing past.
items.explanation: A vague answer sitting next to a precise one from a different stakeholder is a real finding — it can mean the cost is felt somewhere that stakeholder has less visibility into, or that they're reluctant to name a cost that might reflect on their own team. Naming the gap directly, gently, is more honest than building the pitch around only the clearer voice.

items.prompt: What's the risk of building a pitch around only the finance director's sharp answer and ignoring the engineering lead's vague one?
choices: The deal may lose the engineering lead's buy-in, even though their team's cooperation is needed to make the deal actually work
There is no risk — the sharpest answer in the room is always the one that matters most
It guarantees the price will be quoted incorrectly
It means the finance director will withdraw their support
items.reference: A vague answer next to a sharp one is a real finding, not noise — worth naming in the room, not smoothing past.
items.explanation: A deal built around only one stakeholder's clear answer risks losing the buy-in of the other stakeholders whose cooperation the deal still depends on to actually work day to day, even if their answer was less crisp in the moment.

items.prompt: Priya's call had a clean answer at every step. What does the unit say most real discovery calls actually look like by comparison?
choices: Messier — with unclear situations, half-believed problems, or implications that are real but hard to put a number on
Identical to Priya's call in every case, since the four-step flow guarantees a clean answer
Always shorter than Priya's call
Impossible to run without a written script
items.reference: The four-step shape guarantees the right question gets asked — not that the answer will be clean.
items.explanation: Priya's call is a clean worked example, but most real calls are messier: a situation with no single clear description, a problem the prospect half-believes doesn't matter, or an implication that's real but genuinely hard to quantify. The four-step flow only guarantees the right question gets asked, not a tidy answer.

items.prompt: The unit closes by asking what the four-step flow would look like on a call where the real cost is reputational rather than financial. Why is this a meaningful extension rather than just a harder version of the same question?
choices: Because it tests whether the reader can apply the same structure when the implication step can't rely on a clean dollar figure
Because reputational cost is never relevant to a sales conversation
Because it means the situation and problem steps can be skipped entirely
Because it only applies to non-profit organizations
items.reference: The four-step shape guarantees the right question gets asked — not that the answer will be clean.
items.explanation: Priya's implication answer was a clean dollar figure, which made that step easy to follow. A reputational cost is real but harder to quantify, so the extension asks whether the same structure — and the same instinct to let the prospect state the cost in their own words — still works when the answer won't be a tidy number.

items.prompt: In the pitch-first transcript, what specific kind of question does Adri's version of the call never ask that Bex's version does?
choices: A situation question about how many teams touch the work before it's delivered
A question about the prospect's company name
A closing question asking for a signature
A question about Priya's job title
items.reference: Adri's transcript: pitch, then "we'll look it over" — no situation, problem, implication, or need-payoff question anywhere in it.
items.explanation: Adri's call skips straight to the pitch using only the information in Priya's original message. It never asks a situation question, so the three-team handoff — the fact that reframes the entire scope of the problem — never comes up at all.

items.prompt: The unit describes Adri's pitch as "accurate" but says accuracy wasn't enough to save it. What does that distinction mean?
choices: Every feature shown was real and could genuinely have helped, but nothing in the call ever revealed that the handoff problem existed
The pitch contained factual errors about the product's capabilities
Accuracy refers only to correct pricing, which Adri also got wrong
It means Adri's pitch was shorter than it needed to be
items.reference: Adri's transcript: pitch, then "we'll look it over" — no situation, problem, implication, or need-payoff question anywhere in it.
items.explanation: Nothing Adri said was false — the product genuinely could have solved the handoff problem. But since no question in the call ever surfaced that the handoff problem existed, the pitch confidently addressed a much smaller problem than the real one, and lost a deal six times its own size without anyone on the call realizing it.

items.prompt: In the full call transcript, Bex learns work passes through three teams, not one, during which step of the flow?
choices: Situation — it's the very first question Bex asks
Implication — it comes after the cost is discussed
Need-payoff — it's the final question of the call
It's never directly asked; Bex infers it from context
items.reference: The three-team scope surfaces on Bex's very first question — before "problem" is even asked.
items.explanation: Bex's opening situation question — asking how work moves from a client request to delivery — is what reveals the work passes through three teams, not the single 8-person team named in the original inquiry. This happens before any problem question is even asked.

items.prompt: If Bex had skipped the situation question and asked the problem question directly about "your 8-person team," what's the likely consequence?
choices: The problem question would have stayed scoped to one team, missing the cross-team friction that turned out to be the real, bigger issue
There would be no consequence — the problem question works identically either way
Priya would have refused to answer any further questions
The call would have ended immediately
items.reference: The three-team scope surfaces on Bex's very first question — before "problem" is even asked.
items.explanation: A problem question framed around "your 8-person team" inherits whatever scope was already assumed — in this case, the narrower scope from Priya's original message. Without the situation question widening that scope first, the cross-team handoff friction, which turned out to be the real and much larger problem, would likely never have come up.
